### Why the candidate biases cannot be merged In the PyTorch candidate, the input bias is outside the reset product and the recurrent bias is inside it. Their contribution before tanh is $b_{in}+r_t\odot b_{hn}$. In the RNN and LSTM branches above, both biases are added with coefficient one and the forward pass depends on their sum. The GRU candidate has a different dependence on the two biases. Take one coordinate with $b_{in}=0.1$ and $b_{hn}=0.8$. At reset values 0.25 and 0.75, their contributions are 0.3 and 0.7. Replacing the pair with $b_{in}=0.9$, $b_{hn}=0$ preserves the sum of the parameters, but gives 0.9 in both cases. A single constant bias cannot reproduce both values. The reset and update branches do allow the two biases to be summed; this obstruction concerns the candidate branch. The example isolates those offsets. Only the input weight of the reset gate is nonzero. It turns the two supplied log-odds into reset values 0.25 and 0.75; the update gate is 0.5 and the previous state is zero. ```python from copy import deepcopy import torch dtype = torch.float64 biased_gru = torch.nn.GRUCell(1, 1, dtype=dtype) with torch.no_grad(): for parameter in biased_gru.parameters(): parameter.zero_() biased_gru.weight_ih[0, 0] = 1. # PyTorch gate order: r, z, n biased_gru.bias_ih[2] = .1 biased_gru.bias_hh[2] = .8 reset_values = torch.tensor([[.25], [.75]], dtype=dtype) inputs = torch.logit(reset_values) initial = torch.zeros_like(inputs) separate_output = biased_gru(inputs, initial) expected_output = .5 * (.1 + .8 * reset_values).tanh() torch.testing.assert_close(separate_output, expected_output) merged_gru = deepcopy(biased_gru) with torch.no_grad(): merged_gru.bias_ih[2] = .9 merged_gru.bias_hh[2] = 0. merged_output = merged_gru(inputs, initial) torch.testing.assert_close(merged_output, .5 * torch.full_like(inputs, .9).tanh()) assert not torch.allclose(separate_output, merged_output) print("separate candidate biases:", separate_output[:, 0].tolist()) print("same bias sum, different output:", merged_output[:, 0].tolist()) ``` This follows from the candidate equation in [PyTorch 2.14, GRU](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html). It also limits weight conversion between implementations: the reset placement and recurrent candidate bias must both be matched. ## Что выбирать
### Two directions and two sequence endpoints Двунаправленная сеть обрабатывает текст

changes.new: > For the first RNN layer, > the first input is $\mathbf{x}_1$ > and the last input is $\mathbf{x}_T$, > but for the second RNN layer, > the first input is $\mathbf{x}_T$ > and the last input is $\mathbf{x}_1$. > To produce the output of this bidirectional RNN layer, > we simply concatenate together the corresponding outputs > of the two underlying unidirectional RNN layers. *Aston Zhang, Zachary C. Lipton, Mu Li, Alexander J. Smola, [D2L, Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/bi-rnn.html), original English excerpt, CC BY-SA 4.0.* ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/lstm-gru-contracts-2026-11-03/d2l-birnn.svg|Два независимых направления RNN и объединение состояний одной позиции]] *Original D2L bidirectional RNN, Fig. 10.4.1. The two hidden-state rows have opposite temporal arrows and separate parameters. Both states at position $t$ feed that position’s output. The diagram shows generic recurrent cells; using LSTM changes each cell’s internal operations and adds its carried $c$, not the direction of these arrows. Source: Zhang et al., [D2L](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/bi-rnn.html#fig-birnn), CC BY-SA 4.0. Complete pinned SVG, without cropping or redrawing.* For inputs $x_0,x_1,x_2$, the forward recurrence visits positions 0, 1, 2. The reverse recurrence visits 2, 1, 0. The library aligns both sets of outputs to the original position axis: | Original position | Forward state has read | Reverse state has read | |---:|---|---| | 0 | $x_0$ | $x_2,x_1,x_0$ | | 1 | $x_0,x_1$ | $x_2,x_1$ | | 2 | $x_0,x_1,x_2$ | $x_2$ | Thus `output[:, -1]` combines a complete forward pass with the first computed reverse state. The complete reverse pass appears at `output[:, 0, m:]`. For one unprojected layer, `h_n[0]` and `h_n[1]` are the final forward and reverse states. With $L$ layers, `h_n.reshape(L, 2, B, m)[-1]` selects the top layer’s pair. The following program copies each direction into a separate one-step LSTM cell and visits the positions explicitly. This verifies every aligned output and both final memory states, not just the tensor shapes. ```python import torch from torch import nn torch.manual_seed(47) dtype = torch.float64 B, T, d, m = 1, 3, 1, 2 sequence = torch.tensor([[[1.], [2.], [3.]]], dtype=dtype) bidirectional_lstm = nn.LSTM(d, m, bidirectional=True, batch_first=True, dtype=dtype) combined, (final_h, final_c) = bidirectional_lstm(sequence) def trace_direction(reverse): cell = nn.LSTMCell(d, m, dtype=dtype) suffix = "_reverse" if reverse else "" with torch.no_grad(): for name in ["weight_ih", "weight_hh", "bias_ih", "bias_hh"]: getattr(cell, name).copy_(getattr(bidirectional_lstm, name + "_l0" + suffix)) h = torch.zeros(B, m, dtype=dtype) c = torch.zeros_like(h) aligned = [None] * T positions = range(T-1, -1, -1) if reverse else range(T) for position in positions: h, c = cell(sequence[:, position], (h, c)) aligned[position] = h return torch.stack(aligned, dim=1), h, c forward, forward_h, forward_c = trace_direction(False) reverse, reverse_h, reverse_c = trace_direction(True) torch.testing.assert_close(combined, torch.cat([forward, reverse], dim=-1)) torch.testing.assert_close(final_h, torch.stack([forward_h, reverse_h])) torch.testing.assert_close(final_c, torch.stack([forward_c, reverse_c])) torch.testing.assert_close(combined[:, -1, :m], final_h[0]) torch.testing.assert_close(combined[:, 0, m:], final_h[1]) assert not torch.allclose(combined[:, -1, m:], final_h[1]) ``` The reverse output at position 0 depends on all three inputs, so it cannot be used as a causal state after reading only $x_0$. When sequences have different lengths, the reversal must stop at each sequence’s actual boundary. Running backward over right-padding first would allow PAD transitions to affect the valid reverse states. Packing supplies those boundaries; a zero loss on PAD does not. The endpoint contract is also documented in [PyTorch 2.14, LSTM](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.LSTM.html). ### Projection inside the recurrent state У LSTM с проекцией сначала вычисляется

changes.old: ### Разная длина текстов и перенос состояния
changes.new:
Write the unprojected readout as $\widehat h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)$.
The projected state is $h_t=P\widehat h_t$. On the next step, the
four gates receive this $p$-dimensional $h_t$, so the recurrent matrix
has $4m$ rows and $p$ columns. The projection participates in the
recurrence; applying a smaller classifier only after an ordinary LSTM
would leave a different recurrent state.

For the $d=2,m=3,p=2$ example, the parameter count separates into

| Parameter group | Shape | Count |
|---|---|---:|
| Input weights | `[12,2]` | 24 |
| Recurrent weights | `[12,2]` | 24 |
| Two bias vectors | two `[12]` | 24 |
| Projection | `[2,3]` | 6 |

The sum is 78. In the corresponding unprojected library LSTM it is 84.
For general $d,m,p$, subtracting the unprojected one-layer count from
the projected count gives $m(5p-4m)$. Therefore $p<m$ alone does not
guarantee fewer parameters: $m=6,p=5,d=2$ gives 246 rather than 240.
This comparison concerns parameter counts, not execution time.

The full forward calculation below uses nonzero initial $h$ and $c$.
It checks the projection at every step and compares gradients with the
library implementation.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(53)
dtype = torch.float64
B, T, d, m, p = 2, 3, 2, 3, 2
projected_lstm = torch.nn.LSTM(d, m, proj_size=p, batch_first=True, dtype=dtype)
features = torch.randn(B, T, d, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True)
h0 = torch.randn(1, B, p, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True)
c0 = torch.randn(1, B, m, dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True)
library_output, (library_h, library_c) = projected_lstm(features, (h0, c0))

h, c = h0[0], c0[0]
history = []
for time in range(T):
    gates = (F.linear(features[:, time], projected_lstm.weight_ih_l0,
                      projected_lstm.bias_ih_l0)
             + F.linear(h, projected_lstm.weight_hh_l0, projected_lstm.bias_hh_l0))
    ai, af, ag, ao = gates.chunk(4, dim=-1)
    c = af.sigmoid() * c + ai.sigmoid() * ag.tanh()
    unprojected_h = ao.sigmoid() * c.tanh()
    h = F.linear(unprojected_h, projected_lstm.weight_hr_l0)
    history.append(h)
manual_output = torch.stack(history, dim=1)
torch.testing.assert_close(manual_output, library_output)
torch.testing.assert_close(h[None], library_h)
torch.testing.assert_close(c[None], library_c)
assert library_output.shape == (B, T, p)
assert library_h.shape == (1, B, p) and library_c.shape == (1, B, m)
assert sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in projected_lstm.parameters()) == 78

leaves = (features, h0, c0, *projected_lstm.parameters())
manual_loss = manual_output.square().sum() + .3 * c.square().sum()
library_loss = library_output.square().sum() + .3 * library_c.square().sum()
manual_gradients = torch.autograd.grad(manual_loss, leaves)
library_gradients = torch.autograd.grad(library_loss, leaves)
for manual, reference in zip(manual_gradients, library_gradients):
    torch.testing.assert_close(manual, reference)
```

The $c$-state still has three coordinates throughout this example.
A projection neither truncates the time graph nor resets the memory.
Its matrix receives gradients through both the outputs and later gate
calculations. Parameter names, shapes and the projection definition are
specified in
[PyTorch 2.14, LSTM](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.LSTM.html).
